scenario_stem:
Alderfen Supermarkets operates 14 branches across Country X and employs 4,800 people. Four regional directors, based in the capital, each oversee 3 or 4 branches, and every branch manager supervises 5 department supervisors covering fresh food, grocery, bakery, clothing and checkout. The chief executive reviews a weekly written report from each branch passed up through the regional layer before it reaches her desk on a Monday morning.

The board is considering removing the regional director layer and having branch managers report directly to the operations director in the capital. This would delayer the business from six levels to five and widen the operations director's span of control from 4 to 14. The decision must be made before the busy winter trading season, when weekly sales across the 14 branches reach $9.6 million.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'span of control'.
questions.model_answer: The number of subordinates directly supervised and answerable to one manager on a given level of the organisation [2].

knowledge_max_2: the number of employees directly supervised by one manager
can be wide (many subordinates) or narrow (few subordinates) depending on the work

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why widening the operations director's span of control from 4 to 14 might help Alderfen.
questions.model_answer: Reason 1: Fewer layers speed up decisions [k], because branch stock problems currently travel through a regional director before reaching the operations director, and removing that layer shortens the business from six levels to five [app]. Reason 2: A wider span cuts management costs [k], because four regional director posts would be removed, saving salary across 14 branches that already generate $9.6 million in weekly winter sales [app].

removing a layer reduces management salary costs
application_max_2: chain shortens from six levels to five

questions.question_text: Explain two problems Alderfen may face if it removes the regional director layer.
questions.model_answer: Problem 1: The operations director may become overloaded [k], because instead of reviewing 4 regional reports she would now receive a weekly written report from each of the 14 branches [app], so urgent stock decisions could still be delayed across $9.6 million of weekly winter sales [an]. Problem 2: Branch managers lose local support and guidance [k], because regional directors currently visit the 3 or 4 branches they each oversee and understand local conditions [app], so branch-specific problems could go unnoticed until they damage branch performance [an].

knowledge_max_2: a manager supervising too many staff becomes overloaded / span too wide
removing a layer removes local support, coaching and quality checks
application_max_2: operations director would review reports from all 14 branches instead of 4 regions

analysis_max_2: overload slows urgent decisions and errors slip through
loss of local support lets branch problems grow before being noticed

questions.question_text: Do you think Alderfen should remove the regional director layer to create a flatter structure? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Removing the regional director layer would shorten the chain from six levels to five and cut management costs [k], since one operations director could receive the weekly written report from each of the 14 branches directly [app], so decisions on winter stock reaching $9.6 million could be faster and cheaper [an]. However, a span of 14 is very wide compared with today's 4, and the operations director may miss problems in individual branches [k], especially as regional directors currently know local conditions across the 3 or 4 branches they each visit [app], so service and stock control could slip during the busiest season [an]. Overall, Alderfen should keep the regional director layer through the winter at least [eval], because protecting branch performance across $9.6 million of weekly winter sales matters more than the salary saving from delayering [eval].

evaluation_max_2: justified recommendation tied to peak winter trading and branch supervision

scenario_stem:
Caspian Bay Hotels Group operates 22 hotels in 6 countries from its head office in Country X's capital. The group employs 3,600 people. The chain of command runs from the group chief executive through the operations director, 6 country general managers, 22 hotel managers and then 4 department heads in each hotel covering front office, housekeeping, food and beverage and maintenance, ending with team leaders on the floor.

A guest recently waited 9 days for a repairs decision after a burst pipe at the harbour hotel because the request travelled from the hotel manager through the country general manager to head office and back. The board must choose between giving hotel managers authority to spend up to $3,000 locally without approval, or keeping all spending above $500 with head office to control costs across the 6 countries.

Benefit 2: Accountability is clear at every level [k], so after the burst pipe the failure can be traced from team leaders up through the hotel manager and country general manager to head office over the 9 days [app].

Problem 2: Hotel managers become demotivated [k], because they cannot approve even routine $600 repairs without head office [app], so they feel their experience is ignored and may leave for a rival group [an].

scenario_stem:
Emberfall Leisure Group runs 38 casual dining restaurants across Country X and employs 1,450 staff. Its structure is flat, with the operations director overseeing 6 area managers, each area manager supervising 6 or 7 restaurant managers, and each restaurant manager leading 8 to 10 team leaders. There are only 3 layers above the serving staff and no assistant restaurant managers.

Some restaurants struggle at dinner peak, with queues of 25 minutes. The board is weighing two options: hire an assistant restaurant manager in each of the 38 restaurants (38 new posts at $28,000 each, adding one level and costing $1,064,000 per year), or keep the flat structure and give the 6 area managers a $4,000 annual bonus to visit sites more often.

Advantage 2: Lower management salary costs [k], because with no assistant restaurant managers the group avoids the proposed $1,064,000 yearly cost of 38 extra posts [app].

Problem 2: Area managers have a limited presence at each site [k], because each of the 6 area managers covers 6 or 7 restaurants [app], so spending and staffing problems can go unnoticed between visits across the 38 restaurants [an].

scenario_stem:
Hartley Vale Couriers is a national parcel carrier with 9 regional depots, 1,150 drivers and 320 warehouse staff. Depot managers have 8 years' average service, yet head office must approve every vehicle repair over $500, every hire and every route change over 40 kilometres.

Depot managers say the approval process takes 4 days on average, leaving 26 vans off the road at any time and costing an estimated $38,000 per month in lost deliveries and penalty clauses. They argue they are senior enough to judge repairs and shift patterns locally. The board is deciding whether to delegate authority for repairs up to $2,500, local hiring and route changes to each depot manager, or keep central control to protect the delivery budget and service quality.

questions.question_text: Define the term 'delegation'.

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages of delegating repair authority to depot managers.
questions.model_answer: Advantage 1: Faster repairs return vans to work [k], because depot managers could approve the 26 vans currently off the road without waiting 4 days for head office for any repair over $500 [app]. Advantage 2: Depot managers develop and feel trusted [k], because with 8 years' average service they have the experience to judge repairs up to $2,500, and the added authority motivates them to contribute more [app].

knowledge_max_2: delegation speeds up decisions / returns resources to work sooner

Problem 2: Inconsistent standards between depots [k], because each depot manager may hire and change routes differently across the 9 depots and 1,470 staff [app], so service quality and delivery times may vary for customers [an].

questions.model_answer: Delegating would turn 4-day approvals into same-day decisions [k], so the 26 vans currently off the road could return to work and the $38,000 monthly loss could fall sharply [app], protecting revenue and delivery contracts across all 9 depots [an]. However, weaker central control could raise costs and inconsistency [k], because authority to approve up to $2,500 repairs and local hiring could loosen discipline across 1,470 staff [app], and hiring mistakes are hard to reverse once made [an]. Overall, Hartley Vale should delegate repair and route authority up to $2,500 but keep hiring centralised [eval], because repairs drive the immediate $38,000 monthly loss while hiring errors are far harder to undo [eval].

scenario_stem:
Truepoint Engineering Group makes pumps and valves at 3 factories in Country X and 2 in neighbour Country Y, employing 2,300 people. The published organisation chart is functional: a production director, a sales director and a finance director at head office each oversee all 5 factories and the 5 factory managers beneath them. The new chart will be published in January.

The 2 Country Y factories complain to head office weekly about parts delays that can idle production lines for days. The board is choosing between a functional chart (3 directors above 5 factory managers, as now, keeping central control) or a geographic chart (a Country X director and a Country Y director, each supervising their own factories, adding one layer but allowing local decisions).

Advantage 2: Clear responsibilities and no duplication [k], because with only 3 directors above 5 factory managers across 2,300 employees everyone knows their role [app].

Problem 2: Poor coordination between functions [k], because the production director prioritises factory output while the sales director pushes orders, with no Country Y leader to balance them [app], so conflicting instructions can reach the 5 factory managers [an].

questions.model_answer: A geographic chart would give Country Y its own director [k], so parts delays flagged weekly could be approved locally instead of crossing the border to head office [app], cutting downtime across the 2 Country Y factories [an]. However, it adds one layer of management [k], increasing overheads for only 2,300 staff and risking duplicated production and finance posts in both countries [app], which could weaken the functional coordination the group relies on [an]. Overall, Truepoint should adopt the geographic chart with monthly head office reviews [eval], because local control over 2 overseas factories outweighs one extra layer given weekly parts delays are losing output [eval].

scenario_stem:
Corvane Construction Group builds housing estates at 7 sites across Country X, employing 980 people, from groundworks crews to site managers to the board. Its hierarchy has 5 levels: board, managing director, 3 regional contracts managers, 7 site managers and about 28 trade team leaders supervising the crews. Instructions travel down the chain and progress reports travel back up each week.

A new safety rule on scaffolding inspection must reach every site within 10 days. Under the current hierarchy a printed memo from head office took 6 days to reach the site crews last month, and two crews ignored it. The board is debating whether the managing director should brief all team leaders directly by group call, or keep the chain of command intact.

Problem 2: Messages get ignored or distorted [k], because each level paraphrases the memo and two crews ignored it last month [app], so head office cannot be sure the rule is understood on site [an].

scenario_stem:
Solent Harbour Water Co supplies 640,000 homes from its head office and 4 regional offices, employing 1,900 people in billing, field service and maintenance. It communicates mostly top-down: board decisions are emailed to 4 regional directors, cascaded to 60 area managers, then to 214 field teams who read briefings at morning toolbox talks.

After a 12% rise in water charges was announced by letter to customers, call volumes hit 30,000 in one week and only 35% of field staff said they had heard the reason for the rise. Field staff also faced personal abuse and insults from angry customers at their depot gates. The board is deciding whether to start weekly bottom-up feedback sessions with field teams, or keep relying on top-down cascade briefings alone.

Advantage 2: Quick delivery of urgent instructions [k], because a single cascade can reach all 214 field teams by e-mail before the 12% charge rise takes effect [app].

Problem 2: One-way messages cannot answer questions [k], because a cascade e-mail cannot respond to feedback from 214 field teams [app], so problems grow until customers call in their thousands [an].

scenario_stem:

Communication is mostly top-down: targets and safety rules are issued from head office in Country X, and plant managers pass them down. Bottom-up feedback is informal and rarely reaches the board, usually through annual staff surveys. The board meets monthly.

After a Near Miss when a crane failed inspection, an experienced operator revealed he had reported the fault 3 weeks earlier by paper note to his supervisor, who never forwarded it. The line stopped for two hours. The board is choosing between a formal bottom-up reporting and suggestion scheme across all 5 plants, or continuing with annual surveys and top-down safety memos.

Benefit 2: Workers feel valued and involved [k], because a formal scheme gives all 5,200 employees a regular voice instead of waiting for the annual staff surveys [app].

scenario_stem:

The operations director is comparing two options: a company-wide phone app with push notifications, read receipts and rota alerts at $84,000 a year, reaching an estimated 97% of advisers, or improving the written system with paper memos in canteen trays and rota boards at $6,000 a year. scenario_stem:
Oakholt Construction Group builds motorway sections at 6 sites across Country X, employing 1,750 workers, including 260 subcontracted scaffolders and crane crews. Workers rotate between sites each fortnight. Safety briefings were switched last year from 10-minute verbal toolbox talks to emailed PDF briefings for the 6 motorway sections; since then near-miss reports have risen 22% and only 54% of subcontractors say they read the PDFs.

The health and safety officer wants daily 10-minute verbal briefings led by site managers, costing an estimated $96,000 a year in lost working time, versus improving the written system with printed A3 posters and short quizzes for $18,500 a year. The board must pick one option within the next month. A serious accident would halt the whole programme.
